children: Crosspoint Capital Partners is doubling down on artificial intelligence security, leading a $72 million growth investment in startup Mind Security, which helps guard clients against data leaks as increasingly powerful AI agents become widely used.
As corporate use of agentic AI systems rapidly spreads, so do the risks of hackers compromising the technology and stealing sensitive information.

"Now when an agent can crawl your network, and use data, and pass that data to other vendors in a matter of seconds, the attack surface is now very large and it happens very quickly," said Zach Sivertson, the Crosspoint managing director who led the investment. Cybersecurity-focused YL Ventures and Paladin Capital Group also participated in the deal, which valued the company at about $400 million.

In the past 12 months, Mind has seen explosive revenue and customer growth, Chief Executive Eran Barak said. Revenue has climbed 17-fold since a $30 million investment round in June 2025 driven by six-figure, multiyear contracts. Paladin and Crosspoint led that round.
Among Mind's customers are Sony's anime streaming service Crunchyroll and Chinese solar equipment company Sungrow Power Supply.

Seattle-based Barak, whose first cyber startup Hexadite was acquired by Microsoft, started Mind in 2023 with Itai Schwartz and Hod Bin Noon in Israel. Schwartz is Mind's chief technology officer, and Bin Noon, vice president of research and development.
The three are veterans of the Israeli army's elite Unit 8200 cybersecurity division. Mind's main research and development operations, led by Bin Noon, are in Tel Aviv.

Cybersecurity has emerged as a major corporate risk, with detection expenses and global breach costs reaching record highs-averaging $11.5 million in the U.S.-driven largely by lost business, according to a recent report from International Business Machines. Cyber-threat intelligence provider Check Point Research noted a 22% jump in weekly hacking attempts last month from August 2025.

Cyberattacks have been reported this year at the Federal Bureau of Investigation, U.S. water plants and a number of companies. A recent exploit snared sensitive customer financial and personal information from European digital bank Revolut when a hacker impersonating a government official got the data voluntarily from the bank.

Mind, Barak said, monitors real-time data transfers, not just user identities. So while the data request Revolut received may have appeared legitimate, Mind would have flagged-and potentially blocked-the bank's response because it would have stood out as unusual with its large amount of personal data being sent within a short period to an unfamiliar email address.
Guarding against such attacks requires understanding where sensitive data resides and how it flows through a client's systems, Barak said. Mind aims to protect without disrupting client operations.

The company's AI-powered systems scan client networks, identifying sensitive data and evaluating who has access and determining where information is sent and why, so it can better detect incursions. Mind's system evaluates the context of activities it observes, such as client workers querying generative AI engines online.

The proportion of data breaches caused by such "shadow AI" incidents-where workers use unapproved AI tools or personal accounts-more than doubled to 43% in the year through February, according to IBM. AI-driven malicious breaches rose about 56% during the same period and pushed up the average incident cost by about $1 million, IBM estimated.

As autonomous AI agents increasingly operate independently within corporate systems, cybersecurity risks extend beyond human error to include unmonitored machine activity, industry researchers say. Further advances in AI technology could give cyber attackers a significant advantage, unless proper internal controls have been established, Barak said.

With the new money, Mind expects to more than double its staff over the next two years, to about 200, Barak said. The company also aims to more than double revenue next year and reach $100 million in annual recurring revenue by the end of 2028, he said.
Barak's next goal is to bring Mind to $1 billion in enterprise value. "Then the sky is the limit," he said.
